paragraphs: Understanding how a viral population changes during therapy requires a model that can distinguish different kinds of evolutionary change. This paper introduces a hierarchical statistical model for studying that response. Its central feature is that mutation and recombination rates can vary across nucleotide positions, allowing different parts of a sequence to have different evolutionary behavior.

The model also assigns separate parameters to treatment and control groups. This makes the treatment comparison an explicit part of the statistical formulation: the researchers can estimate differences associated with therapy while also representing variation along the sequence. Position-specific rates and group-specific parameters address two distinct sources of variation within the same model.

The authors apply the method to HIV populations exposed to antisense gene therapy and to a more conventional drug therapy. Both studies produce signals described as biologically relevant and plausible. These findings support the method's usefulness for investigating viral sequence evolution under treatment; the reported contribution concerns detecting evolutionary signals rather than establishing the clinical effectiveness of either therapy.
neurips-2008-a-spatially-varying-two-sam.tldr: A hierarchical evolutionary model captures position-specific mutation and recombination rates to estimate treatment-associated changes in HIV populations.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to choose magnetic resonance imaging sequences through automated statistical design. The authors optimize Bayesian design scores to find improved sequences, bringing the choice of measurements into a computational framework. Their approach combines approximate Bayesian inference, statistical knowledge about natural images, and high-performance numerical computation.

A major obstacle is the scale of the inference problem. The models are dense and non-Gaussian, so the framework must handle extensive interactions without relying on a simple Gaussian description. The authors introduce a scalable variational inference algorithm and adapt numerical methods to calculate the basic quantities needed for design optimization. These computational contributions make the proposed design procedure feasible at the scale they study.

The framework is evaluated in a realistic setting using raw data from a 3T magnetic resonance scanner. That evaluation connects the statistical design approach to actual scanner measurements. The stated contribution is a scalable route to automated Bayesian sequence design, with potential relevance to clinical imaging and brain research through better choices of imaging sequences.
neurips-2008-bayesian-experimental-desig.tldr: The paper makes Bayesian optimization of MRI sequences scalable through new approximate inference and numerical computation methods.

paragraphs: Barn owls rely on aligned visual and auditory maps to locate prey accurately. Changes to vision, including prism-induced displacement or blindness, can disrupt that alignment. Juvenile owls can recover alignment by shifting their auditory map. This paper builds a model to investigate a proposed neural mechanism behind that adaptation.

The proposed mechanism involves activity-dependent axon development in the inferior colliculus. In the model, an inhibitory network in the superior colliculus guides axon growth. The strength of that inhibition changes through spike timing dependent plasticity, linking the adjustment of inhibitory connections to the relative timing of neural activity. Together, these components describe how neural activity could guide changes in the spatial mapping of sound.

The authors implement the relevant spatial-localization structures in a robotic system to test and analyze the mechanism. The robot provides a setting for examining how the modeled structures interact during sensory alignment. The contribution is a concrete computational and robotic investigation of a biologically motivated adaptation process, while the biological mechanism itself is presented as a proposed explanation.
neurips-2008-bio-inspired-real-time-sens.tldr: A robotic barn owl tests a model in which plastic inhibition guides axon growth to realign auditory and visual maps.

paragraphs: Kernel methods can represent probability distributions as elements of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Such representations support statistical inference involving higher-order moments, but their usefulness depends on how much information they retain. A characteristic kernel gives each probability distribution a distinct embedding, so different distributions cannot become indistinguishable merely because of the representation.

Conditions identifying characteristic kernels were already available for ordinary real-valued vector spaces. This paper establishes conditions for kernels on groups and semigroups, extending the discussion to domains with other algebraic structures. The central question remains whether the chosen kernel space is rich enough to distinguish every probability distribution on the domain being considered.

The authors illustrate the results with kernels on periodic domains, rotation matrices, and nonnegative real-valued vectors. These examples show why the extension matters: statistical data need not inhabit an unrestricted Euclidean space. The contribution provides a theoretical basis for selecting distribution embeddings on these structured domains while retaining the distinctive information carried by the full probability distribution.
neurips-2008-characteristic-kernels-on-g.tldr: The paper establishes conditions for kernels on groups and semigroups to uniquely represent probability distributions.

paragraphs: Message-passing algorithms working with continuous probabilities need a manageable representation of those distributions. Common options include a restricted family of continuous distributions, sampled particles, or a uniform grid. This paper introduces CAD-MP, which instead uses a grid whose spacing is uneven and whose arrangement changes as inference proceeds.

Uneven spacing allows the representation to concentrate on informative features, such as narrow peaks in marginal belief distributions. The authors give an information-based method for deciding how to modify that spacing. For localizing these features, they report time complexity that grows logarithmically with precision, whereas uniform discretization scales at best linearly. This claim concerns the localization advantage of the representation.

Experiments on simulated data show more precise marginal belief estimates than competing approaches at the same computational expense. The result suggests that deciding where to place representational detail can matter substantially for inference quality. CAD-MP makes that allocation adaptive, using information measures to redirect computation toward features that a fixed uniform grid may represent inefficiently.
neurips-2008-continuously-adaptive-discr.tldr: CAD-MP adapts a nonuniform probability grid to resolve important features more efficiently and improves belief estimates in simulated experiments.

paragraphs: A visual object can be described using several different feature representations, each capturing useful information. Combining them creates a practical challenge because the representations may have different forms and many dimensions. This paper addresses how to map such descriptions into a shared, lower-dimensional space that can support tasks such as recognition or clustering.

The proposed framework, MKL-DR, brings multiple kernel learning together with dimensionality reduction. Kernels provide a way to work with the different representations, while the dimensionality-reduction component seeks a compact common space. Treating these operations within one framework allows the method to consider multiple descriptions simultaneously when constructing that space.

The formulation is built on graph embedding, which gives the contribution a broader scope than a single reduction algorithm. Any dimensionality-reduction technique that can be expressed through graph embedding can, through this framework, be extended to multiple feature representations. The key result is therefore a general route for adapting an existing family of methods to data described in several complementary ways.
neurips-2008-dimensionality-reduction-fo.tldr: MKL-DR combines multiple kernel learning with graph-based dimensionality reduction to build compact representations from multiple feature descriptions.

paragraphs: A visual brain-computer interface speller must identify intended selections from noisy brain responses. Error-correcting codes appear useful because they can make transmitted choices easier to distinguish despite errors. This paper examines why choosing a code purely for its mathematical separation can conflict with the physiology of the responses being measured.

Maximizing minimum Hamming distance tends to increase how often target stimuli appear, shortening the interval between them. Closely spaced responses can overlap, and refractory effects can make individual event-related potentials harder to classify. The authors collect EEG data in a within-subject experiment that varies both stimulus type and codebook, allowing them to examine how these design choices interact.

The results show that stimulus type changes the effect of code design. The traditional row-column code benefits from spatial properties that its target intervals and Hamming distances alone do not explain. Error-correcting codes can nevertheless improve performance with an appropriate stimulus type. The practical implication is that coding and stimulus presentation need to be designed together, with their psychophysiological interaction taken into account.
neurips-2008-effects-of-stimulus-type-an.tldr: Error-correcting codes can improve BCI spelling when stimulus design accommodates how closely spaced brain responses interact.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate quantities such as differential entropy, mutual information, and Kullback-Leibler divergence from continuous data. It focuses on estimates built using nearest-neighbor density estimation. The central issue is how the number of neighbors, k, affects whether the resulting information-theoretic estimates approach the desired quantities as more samples become available.

For fixed k, the authors prove almost-sure convergence of the information-measure estimates even though the underlying density estimates do not themselves converge to the true density. This separates two questions that might otherwise seem inseparable: accurately estimating a whole distribution and accurately estimating a particular quantity derived from it. The latter can succeed under the studied construction despite failure of the former.

When k instead grows linearly with sample size, the information-measure estimates do not converge. Even so, the authors show that these estimates can support two-sample and independence testing. The resulting tests compare favorably with maximum mean discrepancy and the Hilbert Schmidt independence criterion, respectively. Thus, usefulness for a testing task can persist even when convergence as a numerical measure estimate fails.
neurips-2008-estimation-of-information-t.tldr: Nearest-neighbor information estimates can converge despite inconsistent density estimates, and even nonconvergent variants can support useful statistical tests.

paragraphs: Some sequential data contain nested structure: a sequence can include larger units composed of smaller ones. This paper introduces the hierarchical semi-Markov conditional random field, or HSCRF, to represent such hierarchical Markov processes. Inspired by hierarchical hidden Markov models, it generalizes embedded undirected Markov chains within a discriminative learning framework.

The authors develop polynomial-time algorithms for both learning and inference. They also address partial supervision, where only sparse labels are available, through efficient learning and constrained-inference procedures. This is a central practical feature because a hierarchical sequence may contain useful observed labels without having every part of its structure annotated.

The model is demonstrated on recognizing daily living activities from indoor surveillance cameras and on noun-phrase chunking. These applications involve different kinds of sequences but both provide settings for learning structured representations. The authors report reasonable accuracy with both fully and partially observed data. The findings support the ability to learn rich hierarchical models while accommodating incomplete observations through the same modeling framework.
neurips-2008-hierarchical-semi-markov-co.tldr: HSCRFs model nested sequences with efficient learning and inference, including settings with only partial supervision.

paragraphs: A general theory of clustering needs clear statements about what makes a grouping good. Earlier axiomatic work produced an impossibility result for clustering functions, which map data to a partition. This paper argues that the difficulty depends substantially on that formal choice and proposes starting with measures of clustering quality instead.

A quality measure takes both a dataset and a proposed partition, then returns a nonnegative number describing how strong or conclusive that grouping is. This changes the object being evaluated: the theory specifies properties of a score for a given clustering. The authors translate principles resembling the earlier axioms into this framework and add further requirements for meaningful quality measures.

They show that the resulting requirements are consistent by presenting several natural measures that satisfy them. They also establish polynomial-time computation for the proposed clustering quality. The contribution therefore combines a conceptual reformulation with concrete mathematical constructions. It shows that these clustering principles can coexist within a quality-measure framework, giving a workable foundation for discussing the strength of proposed partitions.
neurips-2008-measures-of-clustering-qual.tldr: Axiomatizing clustering quality scores yields consistent principles and efficiently computable measures despite an earlier impossibility result for clustering functions.

paragraphs: Online optimization requires making decisions as objectives are encountered over time. Regret measures the accumulated cost of those decisions relative to a comparison choice. This paper develops a primal-dual framework for designing and analyzing algorithms when the objectives are strongly convex, a structural property central to the logarithmic regret guarantees studied here.

The framework yields what the authors report as the tightest known logarithmic regret bounds for Follow-The-Leader and a previously proposed gradient-descent algorithm. It also connects these methods as endpoints of a broader range of possibilities. That connection allows the authors to derive algorithms between the endpoints, using a common analysis to understand their behavior.

One resulting algorithm retains the computational simplicity of gradient descent while achieving lower regret in many practical situations. This is a qualified advantage tied to the situations considered, rather than a claim of uniformly lower regret. The authors also extend the framework to generalized strongly convex functions. Together, the results provide both sharper analysis of existing methods and a route to new algorithms with useful computational and regret properties.
neurips-2008-mind-the-duality-gap-logari.tldr: A primal-dual framework sharpens logarithmic regret bounds and produces a simple online algorithm with lower regret in many practical situations.

paragraphs: Human motion perception presents a puzzle for standard motion-integration models. Psychophysical experiments find that people perceive rotation and expansion better than translation, while those models predict the best performance for translation. This paper proposes a different inference structure to explain that mismatch between theoretical predictions and observed perceptual trends.

The theory divides motion perception into two levels. First, it selects among competing motion models, such as translation, rotation, and expansion. It then estimates velocity within the selected model. This makes the inferred kind of motion part of the explanation for the velocity estimate, rather than treating estimation as a single undifferentiated problem across all motion patterns.

To support this formulation, the authors introduce prior models for smooth rotation and expansion using mathematical techniques related to the slow-and-smooth model, including Green functions of differential operators. They report good agreement with the trends in human experiments. The findings support model selection and motion-specific priors as a way to account for the observed perceptual advantage for rotation and expansion.
neurips-2008-model-selection-and-velocit.tldr: Selecting a motion model before estimating velocity helps explain human perceptual advantages for rotation and expansion.

paragraphs: When an example can have several labels, a useful representation should reflect the relationships between examples and those labels. This paper proposes a multiple-kernel learning formulation that embeds data in a low-dimensional space. A hypergraph encodes instance-label correlations and directs the construction of that representation.

The method works in a kernel-induced feature space and learns a kernel matrix as a linear combination of supplied kernel matrices. Its original optimization problem is a nonsmooth min-max problem that can be expressed as a semi-infinite linear program. The authors also develop an approximation with a guaranteed error bound, giving a mathematically controlled alternative to the original formulation.

The approximate problem is unconstrained and convex, with a continuously differentiable objective and a Lipschitz gradient. These properties allow existing optimization methods to compute its optimum efficiently. The authors apply the approach to automated annotation of Drosophila gene-expression images and report promising comparisons with representative algorithms. The contribution connects label-informed representation learning to an optimization formulation that is more manageable while retaining an explicit approximation guarantee.
neurips-2008-multi-label-multiple-kernel.tldr: The method learns a label-informed combination of kernels and offers a smooth convex approximation with a guaranteed error bound.

paragraphs: Exploration in control involves taking actions that can reduce uncertainty. When states vary continuously, the learner needs a useful way to represent where additional experience would help. This paper introduces multi-resolution exploration, or MRE, as a methodology for representing that uncertainty and identifying promising regions for further sampling.

MRE uses a hierarchical mapping of the state space. The hierarchy provides a representation at multiple resolutions, and the method uses it to identify regions that would benefit from more samples. The key contribution is this connection between the organization of uncertainty and exploration: the representation helps determine where learning effort should be directed within the continuous space.

The authors demonstrate the method by incorporating it into a prototypical model-based reinforcement-learning method and a prototypical value-based method. In both kinds of setting, it is used to accelerate learning, and the empirical results show improvements over state-of-the-art exploration approaches. These demonstrations support the claimed breadth of the methodology across two distinct reinforcement-learning approaches, with the performance advantage grounded in the reported experiments.
neurips-2008-multi-resolution-exploratio.tldr: MRE uses a hierarchical uncertainty representation to guide sampling and empirically accelerate learning in continuous-state reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: This paper combines convolutional networks with an unsupervised procedure that generates training samples from specified noise models. The resulting image-processing system learns to remove noise from natural images. Synthesizing the training samples connects the learning procedure directly to the kinds of corruption represented by those noise models.

On a test set of one hundred natural images, the networks perform comparably to, and sometimes better than, state-of-the-art wavelet and Markov random field methods. The authors also report that a convolutional network in a blind denoising setting achieves performance similar to other techniques in a non-blind setting. These are empirical comparisons for the evaluated denoising conditions.

The paper additionally relates convolutional networks to Markov random fields through a mean-field theory for a specially designed denoising model. Despite that mathematical connection, the network approach avoids computational difficulties associated with probabilistic learning and inference in the MRF methods. The authors train networks with more than 15,000 parameters while reporting substantially lower computational expense than inference in MRF approaches containing even hundreds of parameters.
neurips-2008-natural-image-denoising-wit.tldr: Convolutional networks trained with synthesized noise achieve competitive image denoising while reducing computation relative to the studied MRF approaches.

paragraphs: Reservoir computing uses a recurrent neural circuit together with a trained, memoryless readout to perform online computations. Such circuits can use analog or binary neurons. Earlier observations suggested that binary circuits depend strongly on their connectivity structure, whereas a comparable dependence had not been observed for analog circuits.

This paper investigates that apparent difference through node in-degree, the number of incoming connections at each node. The analyses include the Lyapunov exponent and examine the transition between ordered and chaotic dynamics. The authors find that this transition differs qualitatively between binary and analog circuits, connecting network dynamics to the observed difference in computational behavior.

The analysis explains the reported reduction in computational performance of binary circuits with high in-degree. The authors also introduce a mean-field predictor of computational performance and show that it accurately predicts their numerical results. Together, these contributions offer an explanation for the observed connectivity effect and a way to predict performance in the studied systems, tying structural differences to the dynamics of the recurrent circuit.
neurips-2008-on-computational-power-and-.tldr: Different order-to-chaos transitions help explain why high connectivity reduces performance in the studied binary reservoir circuits.

paragraphs: Clustering stability selects models by asking whether their groupings persist when data are perturbed or resampled. A potential problem appears as datasets grow: many clustering solutions become increasingly stable. If all candidate models look stable, their remaining differences might reflect sampling artifacts rather than meaningful distinctions.

This paper provides general sufficient conditions under which stability estimators remain reliable in the large-sample regime. These conditions give a way to establish reliability without restricting the analysis to particular toy distributions or specific idealized clustering setups. Their sufficiency matters: satisfying them ensures the stated result, while the abstract does not claim that every reliable estimator must satisfy them.

The authors demonstrate applicability to maximum-likelihood clustering, certain kernel-clustering methods, and centroid-based clustering using any Bregman divergence. They also derive nontrivial asymptotic behavior for frameworks meeting their conditions. This helps explain how stability comparisons behave even when overall stability increases, and clarifies what these estimators favor as a stable model once the sample is sufficiently large.
neurips-2008-on-the-reliability-of-clust.tldr: General sufficient conditions establish when clustering-stability comparisons remain reliable as sample sizes grow.

paragraphs: People often respond faster and make more mistakes after easy trials than after difficult ones. This paper explains that sequential pattern through a mathematical model of response initiation. It asks how recent experience changes expectations about task difficulty and, through those expectations, the tradeoff between speed and accuracy.

The model uses a diffusion decision process in which difficulty corresponds to the drift rate toward the correct response. It assumes that responding depends on the posterior probability of which response is correct, conditioned on accumulated evidence. The authors derive how that posterior depends on drift rate and show that a higher estimated drift rate normatively supports faster responding.

Tracking difficulty from trial to trial therefore produces changes in response speed and accuracy. Simulations show that the model explains several phenomena in human speeded decisions. The proposed account locates sequential adaptation in ongoing statistical estimation: recent trials change the interpretation of current evidence. The authors argue that this passive mechanism provides a more parsimonious explanation than accounts requiring elaborate control structures.
neurips-2008-optimal-response-initiation.tldr: A diffusion model explains sequential speed–accuracy effects through trial-by-trial estimates of task difficulty.

paragraphs: A scoring function orders examples, and an ROC curve describes its classification performance across thresholds. This paper proposes a statistical procedure aimed directly at optimizing that curve. The target ordering is determined by the regression function up to an increasing transformation, meaning that recovering the ordering does not require reproducing one exact numerical scale.

The authors approach this task by recovering level sets of the regression function. They train classifiers through empirical minimization of weighted classification error, then overlay those classifiers to construct a scoring rule. This connects a ranking objective to a collection of weighted classification problems, using their combined decisions to build the score.

The paper proves consistency and derives a convergence rate toward the optimal ROC curve in the supremum norm, which evaluates the largest discrepancy across the curve. The analysis also yields an empirical estimate of the optimal ROC curve. The contribution is both a construction for learning rankings from classifiers and a theoretical account of how the resulting curve approaches its target.
neurips-2008-overlaying-classifiers-a-pr.tldr: Overlaying weighted classifiers produces a scoring rule with proven convergence toward the optimal ROC curve.

paragraphs: Approximate policy iteration uses estimated value functions within a reinforcement-learning procedure. Flexible function approximators can represent a wide range of value functions, but their complexity needs to be controlled. This paper proposes nonparametric approximation with regularization as a way to retain that flexibility while explicitly managing the complexity of the learned function.

The authors construct two algorithms by adding L2 regularization to established policy-evaluation methods: Bellman residual minimization and least-squares temporal difference learning. The regularization changes how the approximate value function is fitted. They also derive efficient implementations for the case where these functions lie in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, connecting the formulation to a concrete kernel-based computational approach.

Beyond defining the algorithms, the paper provides finite-sample performance bounds. These describe performance with a limited amount of data rather than only in an infinite-data limit. Under the conditions studied, the algorithms can achieve optimal convergence rates. The theoretical claim is therefore conditional, supporting the proposed combination of flexible approximation and complexity control within the analyzed setting.
neurips-2008-regularized-policy-iteratio.tldr: Two regularized policy-iteration algorithms combine flexible kernel value functions with finite-sample guarantees and conditionally optimal convergence rates.

paragraphs: Semantic hashing assigns short binary codes to data so that similar items have codes differing in few positions. This paper studies how to construct those codes from a dataset. The authors connect the best-code problem to graph partitioning and show that the optimization problem is NP-hard.

They make the problem more manageable by relaxing it, obtaining a spectral method based on the graph Laplacian. Its solutions use a subset of eigenvectors that are thresholded to produce binary values. This creates a direct connection between the structure represented by the graph and the binary codes assigned to its data points.

A further challenge is coding a new point after learning from the original dataset. The authors use results connecting graph-Laplacian eigenvectors to manifold eigenfunctions to calculate that code efficiently. They describe both learning and application to new points as extremely simple, and their experiments show substantial improvement over state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines a tractable relaxation, an efficient extension to unseen data, and reported empirical gains.
neurips-2008-spectral-hashing-6f4ce9d694.tldr: Spectral hashing relaxes a hard graph-partitioning problem to learn compact binary codes that can also be computed efficiently for new points.

paragraphs: Human choices in sequential tasks often look suboptimal when compared with an ideal actor that already knows how the environment generates rewards. This paper questions whether that comparison captures the learning problem people actually face. It argues that people may also need to discover the structure connecting their actions, observations, and rewards.

The authors represent uncertainty about that structure through mixtures of reward models. They then use Bayesian reinforcement learning to solve the corresponding optimal action-selection problem. This formulation makes learning the reward-generating structure part of decision making, so behavior is evaluated in the presence of uncertainty about which model describes the environment.

In one- and two-armed bandit problems, structure learning produces many qualitative behaviors previously considered suboptimal. Human experiments also show that participants quickly learn and use new reward structure. Together, these results support the argument that some apparent departures from ideal behavior can arise from solving a richer learning problem. The evidence concerns many observed patterns, rather than establishing that all human decisions are optimal.
neurips-2008-structure-learning-in-human.tldr: Learning how rewards are generated can explain several human decision patterns that appear suboptimal when environmental structure is assumed known.

paragraphs: Sparse representations describe signals using a limited selection of elements from a learned dictionary. Such models are useful for restoration, but accurately reconstructing a signal does not by itself address how to distinguish its class. This paper develops a sparse model intended for discrimination, making class prediction part of the representation-learning problem.

The proposed model uses one shared dictionary together with multiple decision functions for signals from different classes. The authors provide an optimization framework for learning all of these components. This connects the common representation to the functions that make classification decisions, placing both within the same learning formulation.

The paper also explains the model from two mathematical perspectives. Its linear variant has a simple probabilistic interpretation, while the most general variant can be interpreted through kernels. Experiments apply the framework to standard handwritten-digit and texture-classification tasks. These applications demonstrate the proposed supervised formulation in classification settings, complementing the paper's representation, interpretation, and optimization contributions.
neurips-2008-supervised-dictionary-learn.tldr: A shared sparse dictionary and multiple decision functions are learned together to support classification.

paragraphs: Cognitive control allows memory and attention to adapt to changing goals and task demands. In tasks where instructions alter which response belongs to a stimulus, people must retain the current mapping in working memory. This paper proposes that those memory representations are inherently probabilistic and that control operations follow from inference over them.

Within this perspective, maintaining and updating working memory are dynamically determined through probabilistic inference. The authors present the model as a compact account of behavioral and neuroimaging data. They suggest that behavior can be understood as optimal subject to limits on learning and the rate of information processing, making those constraints part of the explanation.

The framework also addresses how task instructions can produce appropriate behavior immediately and how experience can subsequently refine that behavior. Instructions and practice thus enter a common account of control over time. The contribution is a probabilistic perspective on the changing contents and use of working memory, supported by its reported ability to account for both behavioral observations and neuroimaging findings.
neurips-2008-temporal-dynamics-of-cognit.tldr: A probabilistic working-memory model explains cognitive control through inference constrained by learning and information-processing limits.

paragraphs: This paper learns matrix representations for both objects and relationships. Matrix multiplication is used to express relationships between objects, but the distinctive step is to also represent relationships between relationships. This allows the same system to handle ordinary symbolic facts and higher-order facts about the relations those facts involve.

The authors demonstrate the approach in modular arithmetic and family relationships. A first-order fact might connect two numbers through adding three, or connect two people through a spouse relation. Higher-order facts can express that adding and subtracting three are inverse operations, or describe a relationship between the husband and wife relations.

The reported generalization includes correctly answering first-order questions involving adding three or the wife relation despite receiving no first-order training examples involving those relations. This shows that, in the demonstrations, higher-order information can support answers about object-level relationships. The contribution is a shared numerical representation that connects these two levels of symbolic knowledge, with strong reported generalization in both studied domains.
neurips-2008-using-matrices-to-model-sym.tldr: Learned matrices connect object-level and higher-order relationships, enabling generalization to relations without direct first-order training examples.
